description: Common foliar fungal disease causing dark concentric target-like rings on older leaves.
symptoms: Concentric rings ('target-board' or bullseye pattern) on older lower leaves, surrounded by yellow chlorotic halos. Leaves eventually wither and drop prematurely.
causes: Fungal spores overwinter in plant debris and soil; splashed onto lower foliage by rain or overhead irrigation in warm (24-29°C) humid weather.
prevention: Practice 3-year crop rotation avoiding Solanaceae family; water at plant base (drip irrigation); ensure proper plant spacing (60cm x 45cm) for air circulation.
management: Prune all bottom leaves within 30cm of soil. Apply bio-fungicides such as Trichoderma viride (5g/L) or neem oil + baking soda spray in early morning. Consult local agricultural extension officers before considering chemical fungicides (e.g. Copper Oxychloride or Mancozeb).
references: ICAR Central Horticultural Research Station / FAO Integrated Pest Management Guide

description: Aggressive disease capable of destroying entire tomato and potato fields within days during cool, damp weather.
symptoms: Water-soaked dark brown/black irregular lesions on leaves with white fuzzy fungal mildew on leaf undersides during humid morning periods.
causes: Airborne sporangia travel long distances; thrives in cool, overcast, wet weather with continuous leaf wetness.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seedlings; avoid overhead irrigation; eliminate volunteer solanaceous weed hosts around field margins.
management: Promptly remove and safely bury or burn heavily infected plants. Apply preventive copper soap or bio-agent Pseudomonas fluorescens. In severe field outbreaks, consult local agronomists for recommended registered protective formulations.
references: University Extension Plant Pathology Advisory / CABI Invasive Species Compendium

description: Devastating viral infection transmitted by silverleaf whiteflies, causing stunted bushy growth and flower abortion.
symptoms: Severe upward leaf curling, yellowing of leaf margins (chlorosis), stunted bush-like growth, and floral drop with zero fruit set.
causes: Transmitted exclusively by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) feeding on plant sap.
prevention: Use 40-50 mesh insect-proof netting in nursery seedbeds; install 15-20 bright yellow sticky traps per acre; plant TYLCV-tolerant cultivars.
management: Spray cold-pressed neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) weekly on undersides of leaves to deter whiteflies. Remove and rogue out infected viral stunt plants.

description: High-impact disease causing necrotic lesions on foliage and tuber rot in storage.
symptoms: Purplish-brown water-soaked spots on leaf tips and margins; white mildew under leaf during morning humidity.
causes: Overwinters in infected seed tubers or cull piles; spreads rapidly through fog and rain-splashed spores.
prevention: Destroy cull piles; use certified healthy seed tubers; practice deep earthing-up (10-15cm soil layer over tubers) to protect harvest.
management: Apply 1% Bordeaux mixture or copper hydroxide preventive spray prior to canopy closure. Scout fields daily in foggy or overcast weather.

description: Fungal rust producing powdery cinnamon-colored pustules on corn leaves.
symptoms: Oval to elongated reddish-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces, which rupture to release powdery rust spores.
causes: Airborne spores carried over long distances by prevailing weather fronts during cool, humid conditions.
prevention: Plant resistant corn hybrids with Rp resistance genes; practice balanced fertilization avoiding excessive nitrogen.
management: Apply wettable sulfur foliar spray (2.5g/L) in early morning. Ensure proper plant spacing for canopy air flow.

description: Foliar and fruit fungal disease resulting in olive-green to dark scabby lesions.
symptoms: Olive-green to velvety dark brown lesions on leaves and fruit, turning scabby, corky, and causing leaf distortion.
causes: Overwinters on fallen orchard leaves; released during spring rains to infect emerging buds and foliage.
prevention: Rake and compost fallen leaves in autumn; prune tree canopy annually for sunlight penetration and fast foliage drying.
management: Apply lime sulfur spray at green tip stage and petal fall. Plant scab-resistant cultivars where feasible.
references: Cornell Cooperative Extension Tree Fruit Guide

description: Bacterial disease causing angular foliar lesions and premature leaf drop.
symptoms: Small water-soaked green-yellow spots on leaf undersides expanding into angular dark brown necrotic lesions with yellow halos.
causes: Bacteria enters via stomata or wounds caused by wind/insects; spreads via rain splashes and infected seeds.
prevention: Hot water seed treatment (50°C for 25 mins); avoid handling plants when foliage is wet; sanitize nursery trays.
management: Apply copper hydroxide + Pseudomonas fluorescens bio-agent. Maintain good weed management to eliminate alternative host plants.

description: Foliage exhibits vibrant green color, balanced turgor, and no visible pathogenic symptoms.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf blade, intact cuticle, clear venation, and absence of necrotic lesions, spots, or yellowing.
causes: Balanced nutrition (N-P-K & micronutrients), adequate soil moisture, and active beneficial soil biology.
prevention: Maintain regular scouting; apply compost/FYM to enrich soil microbial diversity.
management: No chemical intervention needed. Maintain balanced drip irrigation and preventive organic foliar tonics (e.g. Panchagavya 3%).
references: National Centre for Organic and Natural Farming
